---
title: "When LLMs Speak for Groups: Demographic Misrepresentation in Model-Generated Survey Responses"
subtitle: "Working paper, 2026"
date: "2026-11-05"
categories: [working-paper]
authors: ["Martin Lukk", "Neemias B. da Silva", "Ali Sutani", "Abhishek Moturu", "Harris Yang", "Daniel Silver", "Thiago H. Silva", "Matt Ratto"]
venue: "Working paper"
year: 2026
pub_project: algorithmic-fairness
abstract: >
  Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human
  attitudes, preferences, and behaviors in a variety of contexts. Previous
  research finds, however, that LLM-generated responses do not reliably
  reproduce the attitudinal distributions of real populations and distort
  them in ways that remain poorly understood. This study investigates how
  LLMs represent specific, demographically defined population groups and
  how representativeness varies across seven topic areas: health,
  employment, crime, politics, technology use, education, and values. We
  assess how social groups defined by sex, age, education, race/ethnicity,
  income, and employment are represented by three leading LLMs, evaluated
  against these groups' responses to questions in ten high-quality surveys
  covering the contemporary U.S. and Canada. We consider several aspects of
  representation, including accurate reproduction of group-level positions
  and between-group variation. Through experiments using persona prompting,
  we find that the models' group-specific answers are less accurate than
  they would be by simply assigning every group the survey's average
  answer. Across all questions, models are less accurate for disadvantaged
  groups: those with less education, lower incomes, or no work, and racial
  and ethnic minorities. Depending on the topic, models either compress or
  exaggerate differences between groups, and they rarely reproduce which
  groups differ most. Different models also distort groups differently,
  sometimes misrepresenting the same groups in divergent ways on the same
  question. On specific questions, models erase group differences in
  reports of service access and other aspects of lived experience, while
  sharpening differences by education, sex, and race/ethnicity compared to
  survey data. Our findings highlight the potential for significant harms
  when current models are deployed to simulate the attitudes and behaviors
  of specific population groups in high-stakes contexts, including policy
  design and health- and employment-related counseling.
---
